data.title: Paronychia — viva
data.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Paronychia** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Describe the anatomy of the nail unit (PYQ).**
- Nail plate (hard keratin produced by the matrix), proximal nail fold with cuticle (eponychium — seals the space), lateral nail folds, nail matrix (proximal — forms dorsal plate; distal — forms ventral plate; lunula is the visible distal matrix), nail bed (adheres to plate, longitudinal ridges, rich vasculature), hyponychium (beneath free edge), onychodermal band
- Growth: fingernails ~3 mm/month (replace in 6 months), toenails ~1 mm/month (12–18 months)

**Q2. Define acute and chronic paronychia.**
- Acute: painful bacterial infection of the nail fold (S. aureus, Streptococcus, Pseudomonas; HSV — herpetic whitlow) after trauma, hangnail, nail biting, manicure, ingrown nail — red, hot, swollen, tender fold, pus
- Chronic: inflammation of proximal nail fold >6 weeks with loss of cuticle, rounded bolstered red fold, intermittent discharge, transverse ridging/dystrophy of nail — wet work (housewives, cooks, bartenders), diabetes, contact irritants/allergens, Candida colonisation (secondary)
- Drug-induced paronychia with pyogenic granuloma: isotretinoin, EGFR inhibitors, taxanes, antiretrovirals (indinavir)

**Q3. Differentiate bacterial and fungal chronic paronychia (PYQ).**
- Bacterial: acute onset, severe pain, throbbing, pus, rapid course, single digit, Gram-positive cocci
- Candidal/chronic: insidious, mild pain/itch, no frank pus, loss of cuticle, several fingers, wet workers, KOH yeast, nail plate ridging and discolouration (greenish-black — Pseudomonas co-infection)

**Q4. Management of acute paronychia.**
- Warm soaks (water or dilute vinegar/antiseptic) 3–4 times daily; topical mupirocin/fusidic acid
- Oral antibiotics (cloxacillin, cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate; clindamycin/doxycycline for MRSA) if cellulitis
- Abscess: incision and drainage by elevating the nail fold; partial nail avulsion if subungual pus
- Herpetic whitlow — antivirals, do not incise

**Q5. Management of chronic paronychia.**
- Avoid wet work and irritants; cotton-lined rubber gloves; keep hands dry; don't push back cuticles
- Topical potent steroid (± antifungal) as first line (inflammatory/eczematous mechanism), tacrolimus; topical azoles/thymol 4% in alcohol for Candida
- Oral itraconazole/fluconazole when Candida is confirmed and extensive
- Refractory: intralesional steroids, en bloc excision of proximal nail fold (eponychial marsupialisation)
- Patch test if allergic contact dermatitis suspected

**Q6. Discuss ingrown toenails and their management (PYQ).**
- Onychocryptosis — lateral nail plate embeds into lateral nail fold of great toe: tight shoes, improper trimming (curved cut), hyperhidrosis, trauma, retinoids; stages — inflammation, abscess/granulation, chronic hypertrophy of fold
- Conservative: proper nail cutting (straight across), cotton wisp/dental floss under corner, gutter splint, taping, warm soaks, topical steroid/antibiotic
- Surgical: partial nail avulsion with lateral matricectomy (phenol 88% chemical matricectomy — lowest recurrence), electrocautery/laser matricectomy, wedge resection; avoid total avulsion alone

**Q7. Describe the anatomy and growth of the nail unit (linked PYQ).**
- Components: nail plate (keratin — hard keratins), proximal nail fold with cuticle (eponychium), lateral folds, matrix (proximal — dorsal plate; distal — ventral plate; lunula is visible distal matrix), nail bed, hyponychium
- Growth: fingernail ~3 mm/month (complete regrowth 4–6 months), toenail ~1 mm/month (12–18 months); faster in summer, dominant hand, pregnancy, psoriasis; slower in elderly, illness, yellow nail syndrome

**Q8. Candida in chronic paronychia — role.**
- Candida is often isolated but is thought to be secondary colonisation; chronic paronychia is primarily an irritant/ allergic inflammatory disorder of the nail fold in wet workers — topical steroids are more effective than antifungals alone; combine both

**Q9. What surgical options for refractory chronic paronychia?**
- En bloc excision of proximal nail fold (crescentic excision) ± nail avulsion, Swiss roll technique (reflection of nail fold and healing by secondary intention); intralesional steroid into the fold

**Q10. Ingrown toenail — staging and treatment.**
- Stage 1: erythema, oedema, pain; Stage 2: pus/ infection; Stage 3: granulation tissue and lateral nail fold hypertrophy
- Conservative: cotton wisp/ dental floss under nail edge, taping, gutter splint, warm soaks, correct cutting (straight across), proper footwear; antibiotics if infected
- Surgical: partial nail avulsion with lateral matricectomy (phenol 88% chemical, electrocautery, CO2 laser, surgical wedge excision)

**Q11. Paronychia in children (thumb-suckers) — organisms.**
- Mixed oral flora including anaerobes and Candida; treat with amoxicillin-clavulanate/ clindamycin and topical antifungal; discourage thumb-sucking

**Q12. Drug-induced paronychia.**
- Retinoids (isotretinoin), EGFR inhibitors (cetuximab, erlotinib, gefitinib), MEK inhibitors, taxanes, methotrexate, indinavir — painful periungual inflammation with pyogenic granuloma-like lesions; dose modification, topical steroids, antiseptic soaks, doxycycline, silver nitrate/ timolol for granulation

**Q13. What causes acute paronychia?**
- Bacterial infection through breach of nail fold/cuticle: S. aureus (commonest), Streptococcus pyogenes, Pseudomonas, anaerobes (mouth flora in nail biters/thumb-suckers); herpetic whitlow (HSV) is a viral mimic; drugs causing paronychia with pyogenic granulomas — retinoids, EGFR inhibitors, taxanes, HIV protease inhibitors (indinavir)

**Q14. What is a felon?**
- Deep infection of the distal pulp space (closed compartments) — throbbing pain, tense swelling; needs urgent incision and drainage and antibiotics to prevent osteomyelitis/necrosis

**Q15. What are the complications of chronic paronychia?**
- Nail plate dystrophy (transverse ridges, discolouration — green with Pseudomonas, brown/black with Candida), cuticle loss, onycholysis, secondary bacterial infection, persistent swelling, rarely SCC of nail fold (in non-healing cases — biopsy)

## Quick spotter facts
- Bolstered proximal fold with lost cuticle in a wet worker — chronic paronychia
- Phenol matricectomy for ingrown toenail

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Nail disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
